tier_reason: TCHES 2025 paper (Tables 2 and 4) compares against the pq-crystals Kyber/Dilithium ref C (commits 441c051, f1f8085) and PQClean fips202.c (05df469) built with the same Xuantie GCC 10.4.0 toolchain at -O3 on a stated CPU (XuanTie C908 on CanMV-K230, 1.6 GHz); the harness is public on the ches2025 branch (Kyber/ref/Makefile and Kyber/RV64/Makefile 'make speed', sha3/Makefile, common/cpucycles.c) with full flags (-O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -static -march=rv64imac[_zba_zbb][v]) and result .txt files that match the paper.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Xuantie-900 linux-5.10.4 glibc GCC toolchain V2.8.0 (GCC 10.4.0); ches2025 Makefiles use -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -static with -march=rv32imac/rv64imac plus _zbb/_zba_zbb and v variants (-mabi=ilp32/lp64) for both the reference C and the optimized builds; the paper itself states only -O3, -static comes from the README and Makefiles
corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 4 (k cycles): Kyber768 KeyGen ref RV64IM 742k vs ours RV64IM 278k (2.7x, derived from page data) and ours RV64IMBV 165k (4.5x vs ref RV64IM, or 3.7x vs ref RV64IMB 603k; derived from page data); ref RV32IM 1222k vs ours RV32IM 496k and RV32IMBV 284k. Dilithium3 Sign ref RV64IM 8232k vs ours RV64IM 3333k and RV64IMBV 2139k; ref RV32IM 13671k vs ours RV32IM 5069k and RV32IMBV 3054k. Table 2 Keccak-f1600 cycles: C ref RV64I 4926 vs ours 2591, RV64IB 2412 vs 1770, RV32I 15779 vs 7808, RV32IB 12341 vs 6222. Text: RV64I 90% faster, RV64IB 36% faster, RV32I twice as fast and RV32IB 98% faster than the C reference; Kyber/Dilithium 'often achieve speedups of nearly 2x or more' over the reference C on the same architecture.
corrections.caveats: Reference C numbers depend on the compiler exploiting B-extension rotates (the paper's RV64IB Keccak assembly is only 36% faster than the C reference, versus 90% on RV64I, because the compiler uses rotate and andn). The headline 4.5x KeyGen ratio compares the optimized RV64IMBV build with the reference built for plain RV64IM; same-ISA gains are smaller (2.7x RV64IM, 3.7x RV64IMB versus RV64IMBV). The RV32IB Keccak comparison is called 'slightly unfair' by the authors (bit interleaving). Paper comparisons with Cortex-A55/A72 NEON and Cortex-M4 are labelled 'unfair, for reference only'. The repo's main branch has been updated beyond the paper (refactored NTT RVV, SpacemiT X60 support, FIPS 203 alignment); reproduce from the ches2025 branch, whose Makefiles hard-code a board IP and require -static builds. Medians over 10000 iterations except Dilithium Sign (average). Results are for a single in-order dual-issue core (C908, VLEN=128); the vector code targets VLEN=128. MIT overall, reusing public-domain pq-crystals code and Apache-2.0 code from UIC-ESLAS/Kyber_RV_M3. The paper PDF was read through a raw.githubusercontent.com mirror of the author's site.

notes: All Table 2 and Table 4 numbers in the record match the paper; sha3/results_ko_rv32im.txt on ches2025 reproduces the 8734-cycle [Sto19] row. Only fix: last commit 2025-07-15 is about 15 months old, so maintenance is stale, not active. Shortcomings: cross-ISA headline ratio (4.5x mixes RV64IMBV against RV64IM ref), single C908 core, main branch diverged from the paper.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed Nature 2023 paper (doi 10.1038/s41586-023-06004-9, cited in the repo README) reports latency wins over the human/libc++ sort3-sort5 routines, and LLVM libc++ upstreamed the branchless sort3/4/5 after review (D118029); the paper itself was unreachable (nature.com, PMC and a university mirror all blocked), so its figures are known from search snippets only. Not A: the libc++ benchmark code (libcxx/benchmarks/algorithms.bench.cpp) is public but the commit names no compiler, flags or CPU models.

corrections.claimed_speedup: LLVM commit 194d1965d2 (Differential Revision D118029) message: branchless sort3/sort4/sort5 'generated using Reinforcement Learning' achieve 'statistically significant improvement in sorting random integers on test cases from sort1 to sort262144 for uint32 and uint64'; no percentages in the commit (full overview behind a bit.ly link, not opened). Snippet only (DeepMind blog and Wikipedia summaries of the Nature paper): the libc++ changes were up to 70% faster for short sequences and about 1.7% faster for sequences over 250,000 elements, for uint32, uint64 and float on ARMv8, Intel Skylake and AMD Zen 2.
corrections.hardware: Intel Skylake, AMD (Zen 2 per Wikipedia snippet) and ARMv8 machines; exact CPU models not stated in the commit
corrections.caveats: The commit gives no figures, and the Nature paper (the reason for tier B) could not be opened here (nature.com, ncbi PMC, ai.dmi.unibas.ch and reviews.llvm.org all unreachable); the 70% / 1.7% figures come from search snippets of DeepMind's blog and Wikipedia, and per-function latencies were not verified. The repo has no benchmark: sort_functions_test.cc only checks correctness of the inline-asm Sort3-Sort8 and VarSort3-5 programs (int32 buffers), and alphadev.py is non-runnable pseudocode. What libc++ shipped is C++ reverse-engineered from the fixed sort3/sort4/sort5 programs (commit touches libcxx/include/__algorithm/sort.h only for those); sort6-8 and the VarSort programs are not in that commit. Programs were discovered by RL, not hand-written. A later third-party paper (arXiv 2307.14503, 'Shorter and faster than Sort3AlphaDev', snippet only) reports a shorter and faster human-written sort3. Repository archived 2024-08-22.

notes: Record accurate about the LLVM commit (wording, files, no percentages); kept at B on the peer-reviewed Nature paper, but the paper's numbers were seen only through snippets, so treat as a paper-access retier candidate (C if the enricher also cannot reach it). Fixed baseline_in_list to true (libc++'s own -O3-compiled __sort3/4/5 is the category's stdlib baseline). Shortcomings: no figures on benchmark_url, no benchmark harness in the repo, archived repo, an independent sort3 beats AlphaDev's.

tier_reason: First-party comment tables in the perlasm headers compare the assembly with compiler-generated code (gcc-4.4 for ARM Poly1305, gcc 3.4 for x86_64 SHA-1, gcc 4.8 for x86_64 ChaCha), but there is no benchmark harness or C reference in the repo and no flags beyond -march=armv6 for one column, so not A or B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: poly1305-armv4.pl header, 'IALU(*)/gcc-4.4' column: IALU assembly 7.78 / 6.35 / 6.25 / 5.10 / 3.85 / 5.70 cycles per byte with '+100% / +130% / +115% / +95% / +85% / +100%' improvement over gcc-4.4 output (ARM11xx, Cortex-A5, A8, A9, A15, Snapdragon S4); NEON 3.00 / 2.36 / 2.55 / 1.25 / 1.48 cycles per byte on A5 / A8 / A9 / A15 / S4. sha1-x86_64.pl header ('Performance improvement is summarized in the following table'): +45% over gcc 3.4 on Opteron and +65% on Xeon (EM64T) at 6.8 / 9.9 cycles per byte. Newer headers in the same repo: poly1305-riscv.pl 1.8 cycles per byte on SiFive U74, '>100% faster than compiler-generated code', 1.9 on C910 (~75%), 3.3 on SpacemiT X60 (~69%); keccak1600-riscv.pl SHA3-256 22 cycles per byte on U74, '~60% faster than compiler-generated code'; chacha-x86_64.pl IALU column +39% to +99% over gcc 4.8 (5.87 cycles per byte on Skylake, +39%) with SSSE3/AVX paths down to 0.58 cycles per byte on Rocket Lake.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc-4.4 (ARM Poly1305, integer path for -march=armv6), gcc 3.4 (x86_64 SHA-1), gcc 4.8 (x86_64 ChaCha); RISC-V headers say only 'compiler-generated code' without naming the compiler; no other flags stated
corrections.caveats: Performance data is a comment table in each .pl file, first-party and without a harness, C reference or compiler flags; the compilers named (gcc 3.4, 4.4, 4.8) are old, so modern compilers may close part of the gap, and the RISC-V headers do not name a compiler at all. The percentage column is the assembly's improvement over the compiler-generated code (the compiler output is that much slower). The repo README has no performance numbers, and pull requests are ignored (issues common with OpenSSL are redirected there). Some files are old revisions: x86_64/sha1-x86_64.pl is the original integer-only version with no SSSE3/AVX/SHA-NI paths, so OpenSSL's current perlasm is faster on modern x86. The same assembly ships in OpenSSL (and parts in the Linux kernel and XKCP); file headers carry 'GPL-1.0+ OR BSD-3-Clause' or the older 'OpenSSL or CRYPTOGAMS license' wording. Only five headers were read.

notes: Numbers in the record match the poly1305-armv4.pl and sha1-x86_64.pl headers; added newer RISC-V and x86_64 ChaCha header figures. Metadata matches (70 stars, last commit 2026-10-05, LICENSE is BSD-3-style with GPL alternative). Not a duplicate of a listed entry: OpenSSL appears in the catalog only as a baseline. Shortcomings: first-party comment tables, old or unnamed compilers, no harness.
